claims.claim: The Web is an information system built on the Internet, using linked resources and shared standards.
CERN's 1989 proposal led to the first browser/server prototype in 1990; CERN made the technology freely usable in 1993.
A computer is not defined by one historical machine; claims about the first computer depend on criteria such as electronic, digital, general-purpose and stored-program operation.
Stored-program computers store instructions and data in memory, a major architectural transition in the 1940s.
Movable-type printing existed in East Asia before Gutenberg's mid-fifteenth-century European press.
The Gutenberg Bible was an early major European book printed with movable metal type, not the first printed book in world history.
Electricity is associated with electric charge and is a secondary energy carrier rather than a primary energy source.
Modern generators commonly use electromagnetic induction to convert mechanical energy into electrical energy.
Newcomen's practical atmospheric steam engine was installed in 1712 and was used to pump water from mines.
Bardeen and Brattain demonstrated point-contact transistor action in December 1947; the device was publicly announced in 1948.
Semiconductor technology enabled solid-state devices and the transition from vacuum-tube electronics to compact transistor-based systems.
IP provides addressing and packet forwarding while TCP provides reliable, ordered transport; UDP offers a different connectionless service.
Sputnik 1 became the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth when it launched on 4 October 1957.
GPS uses satellite signals and precise timing to estimate receiver position and time.
The first NAVSTAR GPS satellite launched in 1978; the system later became a worldwide civil and military utility.
Paper-making developed in China in the early centuries CE; Cai Lun is associated with an important improvement to its production, not necessarily the first invention of paper.
A surviving historical record of compass use in China dates to around 1119, while knowledge of magnetic north is older.
Scientific inquiry uses observation, testable hypotheses, evidence and revision, but it is not a rigid universal sequence applied identically in every field.
Germ theory consolidated in the nineteenth century through research identifying microorganisms as causes of many infectious diseases.
Fleming observed penicillin's antibacterial effect in 1928, while the Oxford team later developed it into a therapeutic drug.
Algebraic problem-solving predates al-Khwarizmi; his ninth-century treatise helped establish algebra as a distinct discipline and supplied its name.
Zero has both a placeholder role in positional notation and a role as a number in arithmetic.
Indian mathematicians developed the decimal place-value system and important arithmetic rules for zero; the historical record is gradual and complex.
The international Human Genome Project ran from 1990 to 2003 and produced a high-quality reference sequence, not the genome of a single individual.
The 2003 sequence left difficult repetitive regions unresolved; later work, including the 2022 T2T project, filled major gaps.
Renewable energy includes solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal and biomass, each with distinct technical and environmental characteristics.
Binary is a base-two positional system; digital hardware represents binary information through physical states in electronic components.
The term algorithm is historically connected to the Latinised name of al-Khwarizmi, whose mathematical works helped transmit calculation methods.
Calculus developed over a long period; Newton and Leibniz independently developed systematic forms in the seventeenth century.
The history of the microprocessor includes multiple antecedents and competing definitions; Intel's 4004 was introduced commercially in 1971.
Mendeleev's 1869 periodic system left gaps and predicted properties; the modern table is ordered by atomic number.
Biodiversity includes diversity within species, between species and of ecosystems, and supports many contributions to human well-being.
A mathematical framework for studying collections of objects and the relationships between them.
Set theory provides a language for describing collections, membership, subsets, unions, intersections and complements.
The expression of a whole number greater than one as a product of prime numbers.
Prime factorization breaks a composite integer into prime factors, which are numbers greater than one divisible only by one and themselves.
The study of mathematical structures that capture symmetry through an operation.
A group is a set equipped with an operation satisfying closure, associativity, the existence of an identity element and an inverse for every element.
The branch of mathematics concerned with vectors, matrices and linear transformations.
Linear algebra studies vectors, vector spaces, matrices and linear maps.
A mathematical framework for describing uncertainty and the likelihood of events.
Probability assigns numerical measures to events in a model of uncertainty.
Arithmetic in which integers are considered equivalent when they leave the same remainder after division by a fixed positive integer.
Modular arithmetic studies congruences such as a ≡ b (mod n), meaning that a and b differ by a multiple of n.
The physical theory used to describe matter and radiation at atomic and subatomic scales.
Quantum mechanics describes physical systems at scales where classical concepts alone do not correctly predict observations.
A quantum relationship in which a combined system cannot be fully described as independent states of its parts.
Quantum entanglement occurs when the state of a composite quantum system cannot be represented as a product of separate states for its components.
The tested theoretical framework describing known elementary particles and three fundamental interactions.
The Standard Model of particle physics organizes elementary matter particles into quarks and leptons and describes their interactions through the electromagnetic, weak and strong forces.
A thermodynamic state quantity connected to energy dispersal and the number of microscopic arrangements compatible with a system's macroscopic state.
Entropy is a central concept in thermodynamics and statistical mechanics.
The physical interaction involving electric and magnetic fields and their effects on charged matter and electromagnetic radiation.
Electromagnetism unifies electricity and magnetism in a framework describing electric charges, currents and fields.
A device that produces light through stimulated emission, typically in a narrow and coherent beam.
A laser amplifies light by stimulated emission of radiation.
Atoms of the same chemical element that have equal proton numbers but different neutron numbers.
Isotopes are forms of an element whose atoms contain the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.
A selectively permeable boundary that separates a cell from its surroundings and organizes exchange and communication.
Cell membranes are dynamic boundaries built mainly from a phospholipid bilayer with embedded or associated proteins, cholesterol in many eukaryotic membranes, and surface carbohydrates.
Membrane-bound organelles that carry out major stages of aerobic energy conversion in most eukaryotic cells.
Mitochondria are organelles enclosed by outer and inner membranes.
A diverse domain of single-celled prokaryotic organisms with major roles in ecosystems, health and industry.
Bacteria are prokaryotic microorganisms whose cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
Acellular infectious agents that replicate by using the molecular machinery of host cells.
Viruses contain genetic material, either DNA or RNA, enclosed in a protein capsid and sometimes surrounded by a lipid envelope.
The scientific theory that Earth's outer rigid shell is divided into moving tectonic plates.
Plate tectonics explains the large-scale movement of Earth's lithosphere, which is divided into plates that interact at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.
The envelope of gases surrounding Earth, shaped by gravity and structured into layers with changing temperature and composition.
Earth's atmosphere is a mixture of gases held by gravity, together with variable water vapour and suspended particles.
The continuous movement and storage of water among the atmosphere, oceans, land, ice and underground reservoirs.
The water cycle describes exchanges of water among the atmosphere, surface waters, living things, ice and groundwater.
Algorithms that arrange a collection of items according to a specified ordering rule.
Sorting algorithms transform an unordered or partially ordered collection into a sequence that follows a chosen comparison or key.
The mathematical study of networks represented by vertices and edges.
Graph theory studies structures made of vertices, also called nodes, connected by edges.
Database systems that organize data into relations, commonly presented as tables of rows and columns.
The relational model represents data as relations with attributes and tuples, commonly implemented as tables.
A program that translates or transforms source code into another representation while checking and preserving its intended meaning.
A compiler processes a program through stages that commonly include lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, intermediate representation, optimization and code generation.
The transformation of readable information into a protected form using a cryptographic method and key.
Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext so that information can be read only by parties with the appropriate decryption capability.
The long, uneven transformation from predominantly agrarian production toward mechanized industry, factory work and fossil-fuel-powered economies.

The Industrial Revolution describes the transition toward mechanized production, factory systems and new energy and transport networks, beginning in Britain in the eighteenth century before spreading unevenly across the world.
The gradual adoption of plant cultivation and animal domestication by human communities in multiple regions of the world.
The Neolithic transition to agriculture occurred independently in several regions rather than beginning at one universal point.
A historical region between and around the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, home to several early urban civilizations.
Mesopotamia refers to the historical region associated with the Tigris and Euphrates river systems, largely in modern Iraq and extending into neighbouring countries.
An ancient Mediterranean state whose republican and imperial institutions shaped large parts of Europe, North Africa and western Asia.
The Roman state developed from a city in central Italy into a republic and then a Mediterranean empire.
A changing network of Eurasian and maritime trade routes that connected societies through commerce, migration and cultural exchange.
The Silk Roads were not one road but changing networks of overland and maritime routes linking East Asia, Central Asia, South Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Europe.
A devastating infectious disease caused by variola virus that was declared eradicated in 1980.
Smallpox was a severe infectious disease caused by variola viruses and spread mainly through close contact and respiratory exposure.
A pancreatic hormone that helps regulate blood glucose and a life-saving therapy for people who cannot produce or use enough insulin.
Insulin is a peptide hormone produced by pancreatic beta cells that helps regulate blood glucose by influencing glucose uptake, storage and metabolism.
A form of electromagnetic radiation used in imaging because it can pass through materials and is absorbed differently by different substances.
X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation with wavelengths shorter than ultraviolet light.
A field of research, policy and practice focused on improving health and equity across populations and countries.
Global health addresses health challenges that cross borders and are shaped by social, economic, political and environmental systems.
Research studies involving people that assess the safety, effectiveness or other effects of health interventions.
Clinical trials are planned studies involving human participants that evaluate health-related interventions, including medicines, vaccines, devices, procedures and behavioural approaches.
An approach to clinical decision-making that combines research evidence, professional expertise and patient values.
Evidence-based medicine integrates the best available research evidence with clinical expertise and the values and circumstances of individual patients.
The ability of microorganisms to survive or grow despite medicines designed to kill them or stop their growth.
Antimicrobial resistance occurs when microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, fungi or parasites evolve or acquire mechanisms that reduce the effectiveness of medicines used against them.
The study of immune responses generated by vaccination, including antibodies, cellular immunity and immune memory.
Vaccine immunology studies how vaccines activate and shape the immune system.
The processes through which infectious agents move between hosts or from environmental sources to people.
Disease transmission describes how an infectious agent moves from a reservoir or source to a susceptible host.
A field epidemiology process used to identify the cause, source and spread of an unusual cluster of health events and guide control.
Outbreak investigation is a structured public-health response to an unexpected increase in disease or other health events.
The scientific study of Earth's climate system, its variability, drivers and long-term changes.
Climate science examines the long-term patterns and drivers of Earth's climate system, including the atmosphere, oceans, land, ice and living systems.
Computer-based representations of the climate system used to understand past change and explore possible future climates.
Climate models are numerical representations of interactions among the atmosphere, ocean, land, ice and other parts of the climate system.
A stratospheric region containing ozone that absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
The ozone layer is a region of the stratosphere with relatively high concentrations of ozone that absorbs much of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet radiation.
A vast and diverse tropical forest and river system in South America with major roles in biodiversity, carbon storage and regional water cycles.
The Amazon rainforest is a vast tropical forest and river basin spanning several South American countries, with most of the forest in Brazil.
A large tidal mangrove ecosystem in the Bengal delta, shared by Bangladesh and India.
The Sundarbans is a transboundary mangrove ecosystem in the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna delta shared by Bangladesh and India.
Highly diverse marine ecosystems built by reef-forming corals and associated organisms.
Coral reefs are marine ecosystems built largely by colonies of coral animals that produce calcium-carbonate structures.
The permanent or long-term conversion of forest land to non-forest uses.
Deforestation is the conversion of forest to another land use, such as agriculture, pasture, mining or infrastructure.
The engineering discipline concerned with infrastructure and the built environment.
Civil engineering applies scientific and engineering principles to the planning, design, construction, operation and maintenance of infrastructure.
A structure that spans a physical obstacle to carry people, vehicles, railways or utilities.
A bridge is a structure that carries a route or utility across an obstacle such as a river, valley, road or railway.
The planned supply of water to agricultural land or plants to support growth.
Irrigation is the controlled application of water to land or crops to support plant growth when rainfall is insufficient or poorly timed.
The interdisciplinary study of how materials' structure, processing and composition determine their properties and uses.
Materials science and engineering investigates how a material's composition, structure, processing and environment determine its properties and performance.
An electrochemical device that stores energy chemically and delivers it as electrical power.
A battery is an electrochemical device that stores energy in chemical form and converts it into electrical energy when connected to a circuit.
Globalization links economies and societies through cross-border flows of goods, services, capital, people, information and culture.
Its effects are uneven: integration can expand access and exchange while also transmitting economic shocks and widening some inequalities.
Economics analyses choices about scarce resources, production, distribution and consumption at both individual and economy-wide levels.
Economic outcomes are shaped not only by markets and prices but also by institutions, public policy, power, information and social conditions.
Writing records language and information in durable signs, allowing communication to extend beyond the speaker's presence and lifetime.
Writing systems developed in multiple societies; their origins, structures and purposes differ, so the history of writing cannot be reduced to a single invention.
Democracy locates the legitimacy of government in the people and requires meaningful opportunities for participation and accountability.
Democratic systems take different institutional forms; elections alone are not sufficient without rights, pluralism, fair procedures and limits on public power.
Renaissance movements renewed engagement with classical learning while transforming art, literature, scholarship and natural inquiry in different European regions.
The Renaissance was neither uniform nor isolated: regional conditions, patronage, print, trade and cross-cultural transmission shaped its varied developments.
Cervantes published the two parts of Don Quixote in 1605 and 1615, using parody and layered narration to examine literature and society.
Don Quixote became influential in the development of the novel, but the history of prose fiction predates Cervantes and spans many literary traditions.
Human rights are inherent to all people and are expressed through moral principles, national law and international legal instruments.
Human rights are interrelated and interdependent; protecting one set of rights often depends on institutions and conditions that protect others.
Music organises sound through culturally learned practices that can include rhythm, melody, harmony, timbre, improvisation and performance.
There is no single musical system shared by all cultures; musical meaning and structure vary across communities and historical settings.
Ethics investigates how people ought to act and what makes lives, institutions and decisions good or just.
Ethics includes distinct but connected fields such as normative ethics, metaethics and applied ethics, rather than one universally agreed moral formula.
The Bengal Renaissance describes overlapping reform and cultural movements that reshaped education, literature, social debate and intellectual life in colonial Bengal.
The label is contested because it can privilege elite urban reformers and understate the region's diverse communities, political conflicts and material conditions.
Buddhist traditions trace their origins to the teachings of the Buddha in ancient South Asia and address suffering, ethical conduct and liberation.
Buddhism developed into diverse traditions across Asia; doctrines, texts, rituals and institutions vary significantly between communities.
Tagore received the 1913 Nobel Prize in Literature, with Gitanjali playing a central role in the international recognition of his poetry.
Tagore's influence spans Bengali literature, music, education and public thought, and cannot be reduced to his Nobel-winning English translations.
Bangla is an eastern Indo-Aryan language with major speech communities in Bangladesh and India and a substantial literary tradition.
The 1952 Language Movement made language rights central to the political history of East Bengal and later Bangladesh, while Bangla itself remains regionally diverse.
Money commonly serves as a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value, making complex exchange easier.
Modern money includes bank deposits as well as physical cash, and its creation and circulation depend on banking systems, central banks, law and public confidence.
The rule of law requires public and private actors, including the state, to be accountable under publicly promulgated and fairly applied laws.
The existence of laws alone does not establish the rule of law; fair enforcement, independent adjudication and protection of rights are essential.
The UN General Assembly adopted the UDHR on 10 December 1948, setting out 30 articles on fundamental rights and freedoms.
The UDHR is a declaration, not a treaty, but it has profoundly influenced later international human-rights standards and legal instruments.
Darwin's 1859 book On the Origin of Species presented natural selection as a mechanism that can explain adaptation and the diversification of life.
Evolutionary biology developed through many contributors; modern explanations combine natural selection with genetics, population biology and evidence from multiple sciences.
Leonardo combined painting and drawing with investigations of anatomy, mechanics, engineering and the natural world.
Many of Leonardo's engineering concepts survive as designs and studies rather than completed devices, so his notebooks should not be mistaken for a catalogue of working inventions.
Curie's research helped establish radioactivity as a field and led to the identification of polonium and radium in 1898.
Curie received Nobel Prizes in Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911, reflecting distinct contributions across experimental physics and chemistry.
Radioactive decay occurs when unstable atomic nuclei transform and emit particles or electromagnetic radiation.
Radiation is not one uniform hazard: its effects depend on type, energy, dose, exposure time and biological context.
The French Revolution began in 1789 and transformed France's political order through the collapse of absolute monarchy and the rise of new institutions.
The revolution's legacy is contested and complex, including rights claims and republican ideas as well as war, repression, slavery-related conflicts and political violence.
The American Revolution led to the independence of thirteen British colonies, formally recognised by the 1783 Treaty of Paris.
Its language of liberty and self-government coexisted with slavery, Indigenous dispossession and restricted political rights, making its legacy both influential and deeply contested.
Philosophy uses reasoned inquiry and argument to examine fundamental questions about knowledge, reality, value and human life.
Philosophical traditions are global and historically diverse; accounts that treat philosophy as exclusively European leave out major bodies of thought and debate.
Shakespeare wrote for the professional theatre of early modern England, and his works circulated through both performance and print.
The 1623 First Folio is a major source for Shakespeare's plays, preserving 18 works that had not previously been printed.
The Reformation comprised multiple movements that challenged church practices and authority and contributed to the formation of Protestant traditions.
Printing helped circulate reform arguments, but political rulers, local communities, theological disputes and Catholic reform also shaped the movement's course.
World War II lasted from 1939 to 1945 and became a truly global conflict across multiple continents and oceans.
The war's causes and consequences cannot be explained only through European events; the war in Asia began earlier, and colonial subjects, occupied peoples and resistance movements shaped its course.
Ancient Greece consisted of diverse communities and political systems, especially city-states, rather than one continuous unified nation.
Athenian democracy was historically important but limited to a portion of the population; women, enslaved people and resident foreigners were excluded from citizenship.
The Black Death was a pandemic of plague caused by Yersinia pestis that devastated many communities across Afro-Eurasia in the fourteenth century.
Its demographic and economic consequences varied across regions; it did not produce one uniform or immediate transformation of medieval society.
The mature Harappan urban phase flourished around 2600–1900 BCE across a large region of South Asia.
Because the Indus script has not been deciphered, claims about its rulers, language and religious beliefs remain uncertain and must be distinguished from archaeological evidence.
The Mughal dynasty began its rule in northern India in 1526 and developed into one of the major early modern empires of South Asia.
Mughal rule was neither culturally uniform nor uncontested; regional elites, diverse communities, local economies and changing political alliances shaped the empire.
The Language Movement began soon after Pakistan's creation and reached a decisive and tragic turning point on 21 February 1952 in Dhaka.
The movement was broader than one day's protest: it involved years of organising, debate and demands for linguistic and cultural rights.
The Liberation War culminated in Bangladesh's independence in December 1971 after a nine-month conflict.

The war's history includes civilian suffering, mass displacement, organised resistance and international involvement; casualty estimates and some aspects of the conflict remain subjects of historical research.
Gopala established Pala rule in Bengal in the mid-eighth century, beginning a dynasty that endured for several centuries.
The Palas were important patrons of Buddhism, but their kingdom was politically and religiously diverse and changed considerably over time.
The East India Company's victory at Plassey in 1757 helped it secure political influence over Bengal through alliances and the installation of Mir Jafar.
Plassey was not by itself the complete conquest of India; it was one stage in a longer process of Company expansion, military conflict and revenue control.
The Permanent Settlement of 1793 fixed the revenue obligation of zamindars to the East India Company in Bengal.
The settlement did not create a simple or uniform landlord system; local tenure, intermediary rights and cultivators' conditions varied across districts.
The 1905 partition created Eastern Bengal and Assam and triggered major political mobilisation across Bengal and British India.
The response was not uniform: opposition and support reflected differing political, economic, religious and regional interests, which should not be collapsed into a single communal narrative.
The Swadeshi Movement expanded in Bengal after the 1905 partition and used boycott and indigenous production as forms of political protest.
The movement had varied regional and social constituencies; its economic programme, nationalist aims and religious symbolism could be interpreted differently by different communities.
The Six-Point Programme was advanced by Sheikh Mujibur Rahman in 1966 as a framework for provincial autonomy in Pakistan.
The programme was presented as an autonomy plan within a federal structure, although the Pakistani ruling establishment treated it as a threat to the existing state order.
The killing of student activist Asaduzzaman on 20 January 1969 helped turn protests into a wider mass uprising against the Ayub regime.
The uprising was a broad coalition of movements and demands, not a single centrally controlled organisation or event.
The 1943 Bengal famine unfolded amid wartime disruption, severe inflation and failures of food access and relief.
The causes remain debated in historical scholarship; interpretations should distinguish contemporary official findings from later research on entitlement, policy and colonial responsibility.
Rokeya Sakhawat Hossain used fiction, essays and educational work to argue for women's learning and greater social opportunity.
Her work should be understood in its Bengali and South Asian context, including the debates within Muslim communities and wider reform movements of her time.
Nazrul's poetry, journalism and songs made him a major voice of anti-colonial protest and social critique in twentieth-century Bengal.
Nazrul's creative work drew from multiple religious and literary traditions and should not be reduced to a single political or cultural identity.
Vidyasagar played a leading role in campaigns for widow remarriage and women's education in nineteenth-century Bengal.
The 1856 law was an important legal change but did not by itself remove social barriers or make widow remarriage widespread.
The South Asian summer monsoon transports moisture from the Indian Ocean and supplies a large share of annual rainfall to Bangladesh and neighbouring regions.
Monsoon rainfall is not uniform or perfectly predictable; its timing, intensity and distribution vary with atmospheric and oceanic conditions.
The Bengal Delta is formed by the interacting river systems of the Ganges, Brahmaputra and Meghna as they flow toward the Bay of Bengal.
The delta is a changing land-and-water system rather than a fixed geographic shape; sediment movement, erosion, flooding and human interventions continually reshape it.
Somapura Mahavihara was a major Buddhist monastic and intellectual centre in Bengal during the Pala period.
Its architectural influence extended beyond Bengal, but the exact routes and mechanisms of artistic transmission require careful historical interpretation.
Dhaka rose to major political and commercial importance as a Mughal provincial capital in the early seventeenth century.
The city's development was shaped by river courses, regional trade and changing political institutions, not by a single uninterrupted rise in importance.
Silk became a valuable commodity in long-distance trade linking East Asia with Central Asia, western Asia, Europe and maritime networks.
The Silk Roads were not one single road but a changing network of routes, ports and trading communities through which many goods and ideas travelled.
Jazz emerged from African American musical life in New Orleans and drew on blues, ragtime and other musical traditions.
Jazz has never been one fixed sound; its history includes many styles and debates about authorship, commercialisation, race and cultural exchange.
Fine cotton muslins from Bengal, especially the Dhaka region, became prized in regional and international trade.
The history of Bengal textiles includes many different fabrics, techniques and communities; muslin should not be treated as a single unchanging product or craft tradition.
